title: People Rarely Get Credit for the Fire That Never Started
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that organizations celebrate rescues but ignore prevention, even though the leader whose launch never needed saving deserves equal credit. Prevention goes unrewarded mainly because it is invisible: a rescue has a clear problem, a named hero and a visible result, while a fire that never started produces nothing to see. The piece says leaders who want fewer crises must change what they notice and reward, starting by asking team members which problems they avoided. It recommends probing smooth projects, watching for quiet signals such as fewer escalations and less rework, and thanking people for the unseen work. It also warns about the frequent hero who may be the indirect cause of the fire, and suggests running after-action reviews on successes, rescues included.
points: Prevention is under-rewarded mainly because it is invisible, so leaders must deliberately make it visible before they can recognise it.
Leaders should ask what problems the team avoided and what missteps never happened, with the same appetite they show for rescue stories.
Quiet signals such as fewer escalations, less rework and seamless execution point to prevention and are worth exploring and thanking people for.
A frequent hero may be talented but may also be the indirect cause of the fire by moving work forward without anticipating problems.
Running after-action reviews on successes, including rescues, teaches the team to anticipate and head off issues rather than only analysing failures.
quotes: Organizations don’t reward prevention mainly because they can’t see it. A rescue is an event with a clear problem, a named hero, and a visible result.
Prevention produces a fire that never started. Time spent fixing the causes of problems is seen as mundane and expected, not worthy of attention, much less celebration.
Good leaders start by frequently asking team members what problems they avoided and what missteps never happened.
Prevention becomes rewardable once it becomes visible. Good leaders treat the boring outcome as the headline.
Savvy leaders are also wary of the frequent hero. Someone who rescues things repeatedly may be talented, but they may also be the indirect cause of the fire.
That’s why good leaders often run after-action reviews on successes, including rescues, rather than only dissecting failures.
People notice what leaders notice. When a leader is as curious about the fire that never started as they are about the one that was put out, everyone learns the right lesson.
